title: Perceptions and Barriers to Adopting Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: A Survey of Educators in Fifty States
venue: Reimagining Education – The Role of E-Learning, Creativity, and Technology in the Post-Pandemic Era
extended_summary:
This paper examines K-12 educators’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), the barriers they perceive to adopting it, and the kinds of policies, training, and infrastructure they believe are needed for classroom integration. The authors frame the study around broader questions of AI adoption in schools rather than evaluating a specific instructional tool or student outcome. The paper is positioned as especially relevant to current interest in generative AI and other classroom technologies.

The study used a nationwide survey distributed through Qualtrics to educators in all 50 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, yielding responses from 4,528 educators across PreK through grade 12. The survey asked about district AI policies, comfort with technology, prior technology training, openness to new technologies, familiarity with AI tools, perceived resource needs, and access to internet and devices. The sample included educators teaching elementary, middle school, and high school grades, working in public and private settings, and representing rural, suburban, and urban districts.

Findings indicate that most educators viewed AI positively and were open to learning and using new technologies, but they also reported gaps in district AI policies, uneven access to technology, and concerns about infrastructure, training, and awareness of free or low-training AI tools. Comfort with technology was higher among some groups than others, and access to reliable internet was notably weaker in rural districts. The authors conclude that successful AI integration in K-12 will require targeted professional development, clearer district policies, better infrastructure, and equitable resource distribution. The paper also argues that AI should be integrated through an authentic STEM model and used to support, rather than replace, teachers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey with descriptive statistics and no experimental manipulation or causal identification. It provides useful contextual evidence about educator perceptions, but it does not test intervention effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional implications for AI adoption, policy, and training, but it does not demonstrate measured student or teacher outcome gains. Reported findings are descriptive and therefore indicate unclear practical impact rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: Nationwide survey of K-12 educators’ perceptions, readiness, and barriers regarding AI adoption in classrooms, including generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-3/4, Bard, DALL·E-2, and scikit-learn as reported examples of use rather than an evaluated tutoring intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This survey of 4,528 educators found generally positive perceptions of AI and substantial openness to adoption, but also clear institutional barriers related to policy, infrastructure, and training. For example, 64.07% reported district AI policies, 82.53% reported policies for ethical/responsible technology use, and 75.26% said implementing AI would require substantial resources; the study is descriptive and reports percentages rather than inferential effect sizes.
finding.measure: Educator perceptions of AI, district policy presence, access to technology/training, infrastructure needs, and readiness for AI integration

finding.finding_summary: Respondents broadly viewed AI as a potential way to improve efficiency and support teaching tasks, especially through automation, personalized assistance, and reduced administrative burden. However, this was measured only as educator perceptions in a survey, not as observed workload reduction or time savings, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Educator perceptions of AI’s usefulness for administrative tasks, feedback, tutoring, and classroom support
